background.definition: Abdominal pain is one of the most common reasons that children present for urgent evaluation. The goal is to differentiate a self-limited process from conditions that are emergent and may require surgical intervention.

list.listitem: In a catchment area with 173,000 children, 5.3 children were admitted to the hospital per week with a final diagnosis of nonspecific abdominal pain and 2.5 children admitted to the hospital per week with a final diagnosis of appendicitis.
The same study found that the likelihood of nonspecific abdominal pain was 42% higher while school was in session than during holidays.

In a prospective study in Dutch family practices, the incidence of nonspecific abdominal pain was 20.3 per 1000 person years for boys and 29.9 per 1000 person-years for girls (age range 4-17 years). The incidence increased significantly around puberty in girls but not in boys.

In a population study of parent-reported functional symptoms in 5- to 7-year-olds, the 1-year prevalence of any symptom was 23.2% (N = 308). Functional symptoms were more prevalent in girls than boys (27.6% vs 18.8%) and the most common pain complaints were limb pain, headache, and abdominal pain. Among the 308 children with functional somatic symptoms, 21.4% presented with two or more of these functional pain complaints and 4.9% had all three types.
For every 15 school-aged children with abdominal pain, 1 will have a serious condition.
Appendicitis has a lifetime risk of 8.6% in men and 6.7% in women.

The etiology of abdominal pain in children can be divided into intra-abdominal causes (see ) and extra-abdominal causes (see ). A thorough physical examination can reveal extra-abdominal causes, as well as contribute to an assessment of the child's hydration status.
In studies of children presenting to the emergency department with abdominal pain, up to 25% had appendicitis.
Inflammatory: appendicitis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis, and gastroenteritis
Obstruction
Other: ovarian torsion and cyst rupture, testicular torsion, ectopic pregnancy, omental and epiploic fat infarction
Consider the differential diagnosis by age group (see and ), remembering the possibility of sexually transmitted infection for older children and adolescents. C
Use the Alvarado score to identify children at low, moderate, and high risk of appendicitis. B
Fever, bilious vomiting, foreign body ingestion, and blood in stool (occult or apparent) are red flags for a surgical condition. C

Observe a child's behavior before the patient-physician interaction, if possible; this can aid in assessing the presence of guarding or peritoneal signs and the severity of illness. With nonverbal patients, parents will know their child's condition better than the clinician; children often present with a distended abdomen or mass that only the parent will recognize. Parental history and description of the illness is critical.

For children with abdominal symptoms, bilious vomiting, history of foreign body ingestion, and positive guaiac stool test are strongly associated with abnormal radiograph and a surgical condition. RLQ tenderness makes an abnormal radiograph less likely.
Strep throat and right lower lobe pneumonia, in particular, can mimic appendicitis; on history, the character of pain in these conditions is more mild and diffuse.
Helicobacter pylori infection: the history and physical are of little value for the diagnosis of H. pylori infection in children.
Constipation: The child with constipation can have severe pain, both lateralized and/or diffuse, but is usually "crampy" and worse after meals.

The initial clinical impression of a surgeon is helpful for ruling in or ruling out appendicitis, but is not diagnostic. The most common findings of appendicitis in children are fever, RLQ pain, abdominal tenderness, guarding, vomiting, not being able to walk normally, and pain with hopping on the right foot.

A study validated a simple decision rule to determine whether a child was at low risk for appendicitis with 98% sensitivity and 24% specificity. The study found that children with acute abdominal pain <96 hours duration were at low risk for appendicitis if they (1) had an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) <6750/microliter AND no right lower quadrant tenderness OR (2) ANC <6750/microliter with maximal tenderness in the right lower quadrant BUT no abdominal pain with walking, jumping, or coughing.

The Alvarado and Pediatric Appendicitis Score can also be helpful. A recent systematic review found that an Alvarado Score <4 points is strong evidence against appendicitis (LR− 0.02), while a score >9 points is strong evidence in favor (LR+ 8.5, see ).

listitem.strong: Diagnostic considerations by age group are shown below.

list.listitem: In the age group of 0 to 3 months, infants with an underlying critical condition will often present with bilious vomiting.
Infants with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) present with a history of regurgitating after feeding and sounding hoarse; if severe, reflux may be associated with failure to thrive.
Infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis present with a history of nonbilious projectile vomiting that worsens over several days to weeks.
Malrotation with a midgut volvulus is heralded by bilious emesis, poor feeding, and irritability.
Infants with Hirschsprung's disease present with a history of delayed passage of meconium, bilious emesis, distended abdomen, and refused feedings.
Diarrhea and vomiting are more commonly associated with abdominal pain.
Infants with infectious colitis have bloody stools early or as the chief complaint.

Intussusception occurs at a mean age of 7-9 months and pain comes in episodes, accompanied by lethargy. A risk score has been developed and validated that identified age < 3 months or > 2 years, duration of pain > 48 hours, abdominal distension, > 3 episodes of vomiting, presence of an abdominal lump, and red currant jelly stools as the most important independent predictors of the need for surgery.

For adolescent girls, consider gynecologic origins of pain and obtain a human chorionic gonadotropin test to check for pregnancy. Consider ectopic pregnancy when girls present with abdominal pain and bleeding in the first trimester.

Ovarian torsion is a diagnostic consideration in older children. Independent predictors include the presence of vomiting, a shorter duration of pain prior to presenting, and an elevated C-reactive protein.

Consider pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) in sexually active teenagers. One paper reported a decision rule of three variables to help distinguish PID from appendicitis—bilateral tenderness, no pain migration, and no nausea or vomiting made appendicitis unlikely. Although sensitivity was high (rules out), specificity was low (LR+ 1.5, LR− 0.03).

When the origin of the child's pain is not certain, ultrasound is a good test of choice since there is no exposure to radiation and the results can guide further imaging studies. Abdominal plain films can also be a helpful screening tool, but the child is exposed to radiation.

When the clinical suspicion for appendicitis is low, ultrasound can serve as a screening test, with a specificity of 95%. In cases where there is a high index of suspicion for appendicitis or the ultrasound is equivocal, CT scan is indicated because of its high sensitivity. If both WBC and CRP levels are abnormal, that is strong evidence in favor of appendicitis. The Alvarado score (also called the MANTRELS score) has been validated as a method of assessing the likelihood of appendicitis (see ).

For children with suspected inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), the combination of elevated fecal calprotectin and increased bowel wall thickening on intestinal ultrasound gives a 100% positive predictive value in diagnosing IBD with a negative predictive value of 88.5%.
Use of upper endoscopy: abdominal pain is the best predictor for positive EGD (79.9%). Other symptoms have poor predictive value for a positive EGD (<50%).
See the algorithm in for a suggested approach to acute abdominal pain in infants and for the approach to acute abdominal pain in children older than 1 year.
Chronic abdominal pain in children is defined as 3 or more episodes over approximately 3 months or longer. See for a suggested approach to evaluation.
In a large Dutch series, when non-specific abdominal pain was diagnosed at the initial primary care visit, only 3% were referred to a specialist, and 1% received additional testing.

algorithm.title: Acute Abdominal Pain (Child Younger Than 1 Year): Diagnosis.

cell.label: Consider constipation or Hirschsprung's disease (rectal biopsy).
Consider UTI (catheterized urinalysis/culture) or pneumonia (chest x-ray).
Consider: intussusception (ultrasound), gastroenteritis (stool culture, giardia, cryptosporidium antigen), Meckel's diverticulum (Meckel's scan), and cow milk protein allergy.
Consider: pyloric stenosis (ultrasound if 1-3 months), GERD (pH probe), trauma (CT), meningitis, UTI, or gastroenteritis.
Abdominal x-ray to rule out obstruction.
Upper gastrointestinal imaging(UGI) to rule out malrotation/volvulus.
Surgical consult. Consider: malrotation/volvulus (UGI), incarcerated hernia, duodenal web (UGI), ileus, or Hirschsprung's disease (rectal biopsy).

algorithm.title: Acute Abdominal Pain (Child Older Than 1 Year): Diagnosis.

cell.label: Consider ovarian torsion, ovarian cyst, tubo-ovarian abscess (pelvic ultrasound), mittelschmerz/dysmenorrheal, and endometriosis.
Consider PID (cervical exam, Chlamydia and gonorrhea cultures), threatened abortion, or ectopic pregnancy (pregnancy test).
Consider UTI (urinalysis, culture) or renal calculi.
Consider cholelithiasis, hepatitis, pancreatitis, peptic ulcer, or UTI.
Consider gastroenteritis (consider Rotazyme, stool culture, cryptosporidium antigen, Giardia antigen), inflammatory bowel disease, or lactose intolerance.
Calculate Alvarado Score Rule 364: 1 point each for RLQ pain, anorexia, nausea/vomiting, rebound pain, temp >99.1ºF, WBC >10.0, and left shift. Add 2 points for RLQ tenderness.
Consider pneumonia (chest x-ray), UTI (urinalysis/culture), appendicitis (CT or ultrasound), gastroenteritis, or pharyngitis (rapid strep, monospot).
Order abdominal CT and consider abuse.

Child with functional abdominal pain; that is, pain for more than 6 months, may be intermittent or persistent, and presumes that anatomic, infectious, inflammatory, and metabolic processes have been ruled out with no alarm symptoms.*
Evaluate as for acute abdominal pain in.
Features of migraine: (maternal migraine history, paroxysmal pain, anorexia, nausea, vomiting or pallor)?
If not improved, consider referral to pediatric gastroenterologist.
Check H. pylori and consider H2 blocker or proton pump inhibitor.
Consider anti-spasmodics, nonstimulant laxatives, and anti-diarrheals.
Appropriate migraine treatment consistent with age.

footnotes.footnote: *Alarm symptoms include abdominal mass, positive fecal occult blood testing, jaundice, bacteruria, fever, abnormal exam, or abnormal blood tests.
